text: There happened to be a troublemaker there named Sheba son of Bichri, a Benjaminite, who blew the trumpet and shouted that they had no share in David and no inheritance in Jesse's son — every man to his tents, O Israel!
So all of Israel's men abandoned David to follow Sheba son of Bichri, while Judah's men stayed loyally with their king all the way from the Jordan to Jerusalem.

David reached his house in Jerusalem and took the ten concubines he had left to look after the palace, put them under guard in a separate house, and provided for them, but never went in to them again — they lived shut away like widows until they died.
The king told Amasa to summon Judah's men to him within three days, and to be present himself.
So Amasa went to call up Judah, but he took longer than the time David had set for him.
David told Abishai that Sheba son of Bichri would cause them more trouble than Absalom had, and ordered him to take his men and chase Sheba down before he could find walled cities and get away.
So Joab's men, the Cherethites and Pelethites, and all the mighty warriors went out from Jerusalem after Sheba son of Bichri.
When they reached the great stone at Gibeon, Amasa came to meet them; Joab was dressed for battle with a sword strapped to his thigh in its sheath, and as he stepped forward it slipped out.
Joab asked Amasa if all was well with him, my brother, and took hold of his beard with his right hand as if to kiss him.

Amasa never noticed the sword in Joab's other hand, and Joab drove it into his stomach, spilling his insides onto the ground — one blow was enough, and he died; then Joab and his brother Abishai went on after Sheba son of Bichri.
One of Joab's men stood over Amasa's body calling out that whoever was for Joab and for David should follow after Joab.
Amasa's body lay in the middle of the road soaked in blood, and when the man saw that everyone stopped to stare, he dragged the body off the road into a field and threw a cloak over it.
Once the body was off the road, the whole army moved on after Joab to hunt down Sheba son of Bichri.
Sheba passed through all the tribes of Israel until he reached Abel Beth-maacah, and all his own clan, the Bichrites, gathered and followed him inside.
Joab's whole force arrived and laid siege to him at Abel Beth-maacah, building a ramp against the city and battering the wall to bring it down.
Then a woman known for her wisdom called out from the city, asking someone to tell Joab to come near so she could speak with him.
When Joab came close, she asked if he was Joab, and he confirmed it was him; she asked him to listen to his servant, and he said he was listening.
She said people used to say that if you wanted to settle a dispute, you simply asked for counsel at Abel.
She described herself as one of the peaceful and loyal people of Israel, and asked why he wanted to destroy a city that was like a mother in Israel — why swallow up the LORD's own inheritance?
Joab insisted that was never his intention, that he had no wish to destroy or swallow anything up.

He explained that a man from the hill country of Ephraim named Sheba son of Bichri had rebelled against King David, and that if they handed him over alone, he would withdraw from the city; the woman promised his head would be thrown to Joab over the wall.

The woman then went to the people with her plan, and they cut off Sheba son of Bichri's head and threw it out to Joab, who sounded the retreat, and the army dispersed to their homes while Joab returned to the king in Jerusalem.
Joab was again in command of Israel's whole army, and Benaiah son of Jehoiada commanded the Cherethites and Pelethites.
Adoram supervised the forced labor gangs, and Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud kept the royal records.
Sheva served as secretary, while Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
And Ira the Jairite also served as a priest to David.
